overview.summary: Vectors (or Dynamic Arrays) are arrays that automatically resize themselves when they run out of space.
learningObjectives: Understand the difference between Logical Size and Physical Capacity.
Explain the O(N) cost of resizing.
Understand why append operations are 'Amortized O(1)'.
overview.interviewRelevance: Dynamic arrays are the default 'list' structure in Python, JS, and C++. Knowing how they resize is a classic conceptual interview question.

paragraphs: Imagine hosting a party in a small room. More guests arrive until the room is completely full. You can't just 'expand' the walls.
Instead, you rent a room twice as big next door, ask everyone to walk over to the new room, and then resume the party. This is exactly how dynamic arrays handle running out of memory.
realWorldHook.ahaMoment: A dynamic array is just a regular static array under the hood. It fakes being 'dynamic' by secretly creating larger static arrays and copying data over when needed.

definition.technicalDefinition: A Dynamic Array (Vector in C++, ArrayList in Java, List in Python) is a random access, variable-size list data structure that allows elements to be added or removed.

vocabulary.definition: The number of elements currently stored in the vector.
The actual size of the underlying memory block.
An average time complexity that accounts for occasional expensive operations spread out over many fast operations.

keyProperties: O(1) amortized insertion at the end.
O(N) insertion/deletion in the middle (due to shifting elements).

metaphor: A hermit crab finding a new shell. When it outgrows its current shell, it leaves it behind and moves into a shell twice as large.
mentalModel.clickSentence: By doubling the capacity every time we run out of space, the heavy O(N) cost of copying elements happens so rarely that the average cost per insert drops to O(1).

memoryDescription: In memory, a Vector keeps track of a pointer to the start of the array, the current 'Size', and the current 'Capacity'.
When Size == Capacity, the Vector allocates a new chunk of memory of size Capacity * 2, copies the old elements over, and frees the old chunk.

definitionCode.python:
arr = [] # Python lists are dynamic arrays
arr.append(1)
definitionCode.javascript:
const arr = []; // JS arrays are dynamic
arr.push(1);

memoryLayout.label: Capacity
memoryLayout.value: 8 (It doubled when the 4th item was added)

steps.explanation: Start with an empty vector of capacity 2. Empty slots are shown as ·.
Write 4 into slot 0. Size is now 1.
Write 8 into slot 1. Size is now 2.
Full! Pushing 15 needs room, so allocate a new block of capacity 4.
Copy all 2 elements into the bigger block. This O(n) copy is rare, so push stays O(1) amortized.
Write 15 into slot 2. Size is now 3.
Write 16 into slot 3. Size is now 4.
Full! Pushing 23 needs room, so allocate a new block of capacity 8.
Copy all 4 elements into the bigger block. This O(n) copy is rare, so push stays O(1) amortized.
Write 23 into slot 4. Size is now 5.

operations.name: Append (Push Back)
operations.description: Add an element to the end. If capacity is full, double the array size first.
operations.visualNote: A new cell is filled. Occasionally, the entire array gets copied to a larger block.

operations.name: Insert Middle
operations.description: Insert at a specific index. Requires shifting all subsequent elements to the right.
operations.visualNote: Elements slide to the right to make room.

patternTemplate.whenToUse: Whenever you need an array but you do not know how many elements you will need to store ahead of time.

recognitionQuiz.problemStatement: You are reading a file line by line and storing all lines that contain the word 'Error'. You don't know the file size.
recognitionQuiz.explanation: Because you don't know the final size, a static array will fail. A dynamic array (Vector) will automatically resize as you append.

examples.title: Design Dynamic Array
steps: Create variables for size, capacity, and the actual array.
Implement pushback: check if size == capacity. If so, create a new array double the size.
examples.spaceComplexity: O(N) for the new array during resize
examples.rationale: This explicitly shows the hidden O(N) copy operation that happens behind the scenes in languages like Python.

conceptQuiz.question: What does 'Amortized O(1)' mean?
options: The average time per operation is O(1) when spread out over many operations, even if one operation takes O(N).
It means O(1) in the worst case.
It means the operation is instantly fast.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Because you double the capacity, you do an O(N) copy, but then you get N free O(1) operations. So the average cost is exactly O(1).

conceptQuiz.question: Why not just increase the capacity by 1 each time instead of doubling it?
options: Because adding 1 would require copying the entire array every single time you append, making appending O(N).
Because computers only understand powers of 2.
conceptQuiz.explanation: If you increased capacity by 1, you would do an O(N) copy for every single insert, resulting in an O(N^2) total time for N inserts. Doubling guarantees O(N) total time for N inserts.

practice.title: Design Dynamic Array (Concept)
practice.keyInsight: Understand the internal copy mechanisms of your language's array.
